ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — John F. Kennedy

code.originalText: Establishing primary care about three months after primary adrenal insufficiency was diagnosed during an adrenal crisis abroad: replacement doses, electrolytes and renin, cause, autoimmune screening, sick-day rules and emergency kit, and chronic low back pain

text.paragraph: Establishing primary care about three months after primary adrenal insufficiency was diagnosed during an adrenal crisis abroad: replacement doses, electrolytes and renin, cause, autoimmune screening, sick-day rules and emergency kit, and chronic low back pain [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: He wants to understand his adrenal condition and to never again be as ill as he was abroad. [S]
He wants enough energy to keep a full working week, and to decide himself who knows about the diagnosis. [S]
He wants his back pain to stop limiting him and to rely less on the brace. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: John F. Kennedy was born on May 29, 1917, in Brookline, Massachusetts. [D]

A few months before his third birthday he had a serious case of scarlet fever and spent a month in the hospital; through childhood and adolescence he had nausea, joint pain, headaches and diarrhea and was hospitalized several times. [D]
By 1934 he was sent to the Mayo Clinic, where his bowel illness was diagnosed as colitis. [D]
During his college years at Harvard his abdominal pain, weight loss and weakness continued despite a bland diet and strong medicines, including steroids placed under the skin to dissolve. [D]

The historian Robert Dallek, who examined his medical records at the Kennedy Library, believed that many of his difficulties could be traced to corticosteroids taken perhaps as early as 1937 to relieve his colitis, noting that heavy long-term use can promote osteoporosis. [R]
His chronic back pain began at Harvard, after he was tackled from the side in a football game, possibly damaging a spinal disc; he began wearing a corset brace to stabilize his spine. [D]

His back and intestinal problems caused him to fail Army and Navy physical examinations, but he was admitted to the Navy in October 1941. In August 1943 the patrol torpedo boat he commanded, PT-109, was struck by a Japanese destroyer; he led the survivors to safety, and his back worsened as a result. [D]
He came home from the war in the Pacific thin and sallow from malaria. [D]
Against the advice of his doctors at the Mayo Clinic, he had spinal surgery in June 1944 at New England Baptist Hospital; about six weeks later the pain returned. [D]
In 1946, at 29, he was elected to the U.S. House of Representatives from a Boston district. During the campaign his back was so bad that he wore a brace and used daily hot baths and massage. [D]
In 1947, at 30, while a congressman, he collapsed on a visit to England; a doctor there diagnosed Addison's disease and told one of his friends that he might not live a year. [D]
Returning to America aboard the Queen Mary, he was so ill that a priest was called to give him the last rites. [D]

He passed off the illness as a recurrence of his wartime malaria. In Boston an endocrinologist began treating him for Addison's disease with pellets of a synthetic adrenal hormone, desoxycorticosterone acetate (DOCA), implanted under his skin. [D]
Macchia and colleagues proposed that his bowel symptoms from adolescence fit well with coeliac disease. [R]

text.paragraph: 11 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
Historical biography with true dates. These events are not part of the synthetic care timeline.

list.item: First-term member of the U.S. House of Representatives; travels each week between Washington and his district in Boston; long days with speeches and meetings, often with irregular meals [S]
Single; lives in a rented house in Washington with a household staff member who helps with errands [S]
Tobacco: none. Alcohol: one or two drinks at social events, not every week. No drug use [S]
Activity: swims when he can, which eases his back; walks little because of the pain [S]
Supports: close friends he trusts, colleagues who cover for him on bad days, and work he finds meaningful; swimming eases his back [S]
He wants to decide himself who is told about his diagnosis; his office staff know only that he has a chronic condition that needs daily tablets [S]

tr.td: Hydrocortisone 10 mg oral tablet, two tablets (20 mg) on waking and one tablet (10 mg) at 2 pm, 30 mg a day (started in hospital)
Two tablets on waking and one tablet at 2 pm
Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg oral tablet, half a tablet (0.05 mg) by mouth once daily (started in hospital)
Half a tablet by mouth once daily
Hydrocortisone 100 mg injection kit (with diluent), 100 mg into the thigh muscle once for vomiting, collapse or signs of adrenal crisis, then call 911
Once, as needed for adrenal crisis; carry at all times
Acetaminophen 500 mg oral tablet, two tablets by mouth up to three times a day as needed for back pain
Two tablets up to three times a day as needed

text.paragraph: Positive for the concerns in the history of present illness. Alert, oriented and good-humored; describes his mood as tired but well; no low mood or loss of interest; PHQ-9 score 4, mainly tiredness. No other systems reported as affected in this synthetic episode. [S]

list.item: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease), diagnosed about three months ago during an adrenal crisis while traveling abroad, on hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone; synthetic modern episode linked to his documented 1947 diagnosis: active, confirmed [S]

Chronic low back pain persisting after lumbar disc surgery; began after a football injury in college and worsened during wartime naval service; uses a corset brace; synthetic modern episode linked to his documented back history: active, confirmed [S]
Raised TSH with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies and normal free T4 on screening for associated autoimmune disease; to be repeated before any treatment: active, confirmed [S]

Glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement adjusted by clinical assessment at every visit (weight, blood pressure lying and standing, energy, salt craving, and signs of over- or under-replacement), with sodium, potassium and plasma renin to guide fludrocortisone; doses set with endocrinology. Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (2016) [S]

Endocrinology consultation to confirm the cause, set the replacement doses, review the thyroid results and bone health, and plan stress dosing and follow-up. Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (2016) [S]

Written sick-day rules (double the hydrocortisone for fever above 38 °C, triple it above 39 °C, and inject and seek emergency care if vomiting or unable to take tablets), an emergency hydrocortisone injection kit with training, a steroid emergency card and a medical ID, reviewed at every visit. Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (2016) [S]

Screening for associated autoimmune disease: 21-hydroxylase antibodies for the cause, TSH, free T4 and thyroid peroxidase antibodies, vitamin B12, A1c and celiac serology with total IgA at intake; TSH at least yearly afterwards, and the others yearly or with symptoms. Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (2016); American College of Gastroenterology Guidelines Update: Diagnosis and Management of Celiac Disease (2023); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, hypothyroidism monograph (2026) [S]

Chronic low back pain: physical therapy with core strengthening, swimming, heat, and gradual weaning from the brace except on long journeys; acetaminophen as needed; no opioids; Oswestry Disability Index at each review; imaging only for red flags. Guideline: Noninvasive Treatments for Acute, Subacute, and Chronic Low Back Pain: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians (2017) [S]

Bone health: a bone density scan because of corticosteroid exposure in his teens and twenties, calcium and vitamin D from diet, weight-bearing exercise, and avoiding glucocorticoid over-replacement. Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency: An Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (2016); 2022 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for the Prevention and Treatment of Glucocorticoid-Induced Osteoporosis (2022); Osteoporosis in men: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline (2012) [S]
